PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 90 — Lesson 114: Diabetic Foot Ulcer, Infection & Limb Preservation

FNP-level goal: Treat the diabetic foot as an interaction among neuropathy, pressure, deformity, ischemia, skin breakdown, and infection; identify urgent threats to limb and life; and coordinate prevention, offloading, wound care, vascular assessment, and specialty referral.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain how loss of protective sensation, biomechanical pressure, peripheral artery disease, and infection combine to create diabetes-related foot ulcers and amputation risk.
  • Perform and document a focused foot assessment: skin and nails, wound characteristics, pulses/perfusion, sensation, structure, footwear, function, and infection severity.
  • Recognize when ulceration, infection, ischemia, suspected osteomyelitis, or active Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy requires urgent multidisciplinary evaluation.
  • Differentiate treatment of infection from treatment of pressure, ischemia, neuropathy, and poor wound healing.
  • Teach patient-centered daily foot protection without blame, and establish a practical follow-up and referral plan.

Part 1 — The Limb-Preservation Model

A diabetic foot ulcer is rarely caused by one isolated event. Diabetes-related peripheral neuropathy can reduce pain and pressure sensation; a patient may not notice a blister, foreign object, tight shoe, or repetitive loading. Foot deformity and limited joint motion concentrate pressure. Peripheral artery disease (PAD) reduces perfusion and healing capacity. Infection can then spread through vulnerable tissue. The clinical task is to identify which parts of this chain are active in this patient today.

Do not assume that absence of pain means absence of danger. Loss of protective sensation may make a deep ulcer painless. Conversely, new pain in a patient with neuropathy may signal infection, ischemia, fracture, or Charcot change and deserves attention. Limb preservation begins before an ulcer occurs: prevention is active clinical care, not a handout given once a year.

Part 2 — The Comprehensive Foot Assessment

At diabetes visits, a basic foot check can uncover emerging problems; a comprehensive periodic assessment is especially important for patients at risk. Inspect dorsal, plantar, interdigital, heel, and nail surfaces. Look for skin breaks, maceration, fissures, callus, erythema, drainage, blisters, fungal disease, deformity, edema, temperature asymmetry, prior amputation, and shoe friction.

Assess pulses and overall perfusion, sensation using an appropriate standardized approach within your setting, foot structure and gait when feasible, footwear, self-care ability, and history of ulcer, amputation, revascularization, smoking, renal disease, or prior infection. Documentation should tell the next clinician what changed: location, dimensions, depth, tissue appearance, drainage, odor, surrounding skin, pain, perfusion, sensation, and functional impact.

Part 3 — Neuropathy: Loss of Protective Sensation Changes Everything

Neuropathy can present as numbness, burning, tingling, allodynia, altered temperature sensation, or no symptoms at all. The absence of symptoms is not reassurance. When protective sensation is reduced, a patient may continue walking on a wound because it does not hurt. Repetitive plantar pressure then prevents healing and extends tissue damage.

Explain this mechanism in plain language: a painless foot is not necessarily a safe foot. Encourage daily inspection using a mirror or help from another person if vision, mobility, or body habitus limits self-examination. Advise against walking barefoot, self-treating corns or calluses with caustic products, or soaking a vulnerable foot without individualized guidance. The aim is autonomy and prevention, not fear.

Part 4 — Ischemia: An Ulcer Cannot Heal Without Adequate Blood Flow

PAD can coexist with neuropathy and may be underrecognized because neuropathy masks ischemic pain. Ask about exertional leg symptoms, rest pain, prior vascular procedures, tobacco exposure, nonhealing wounds, and change in color or temperature. Examine pulses, capillary and skin features in context, and compare limbs. A normal-looking foot does not exclude vascular disease, and an apparently minor ulcer can become limb-threatening when perfusion is poor.

When an ulcer, gangrene, or nonhealing wound raises concern for ischemia, the question is not simply whether to add an antibiotic. The patient may need timely vascular assessment and consideration of revascularization. Infection plus ischemia is particularly dangerous because both healing and antibiotic delivery can be compromised.

Part 5 — Describe the Ulcer Before You Name the Plan

For every ulcer, document exact location, length and width, depth or exposed structure if visible, wound bed, undermining or tunneling, drainage amount and quality, odor, periwound skin, pain, edema, infection signs, and perfusion. A plantar callused ulcer suggests pressure and offloading needs; an ischemic ulcer may have a different appearance and urgency. A wound photograph can be clinically useful only with proper consent, secure workflow, consistent technique, and local policy.

Ulcer classification systems can improve shared language, but they do not replace judgment. They should prompt the team to ask: Is this infected? Is it ischemic? Is bone or deeper tissue involved? Is pressure being removed? Can this patient realistically perform the plan and return on time?

Part 6 — Infection Is a Clinical Diagnosis

Do not diagnose diabetic foot infection from a wound culture alone. Colonization is common in chronic wounds. Diagnose infection clinically from local or systemic inflammatory features in the full context of the patient. Evaluate for purulence, increasing erythema, warmth, swelling, tenderness, induration, malodor, lymphangitic spread, systemic symptoms, and functional decline. Neuropathy or immunologic impairment can mute classic findings, so worsening drainage, tissue discoloration, unexpected glucose deterioration, or a new odor may matter.

When infection is present, assess severity and the need for urgent drainage, imaging, cultures from appropriate tissue, surgical consultation, admission, or parenteral therapy according to current protocols and local resources. Antibiotics are selected for a clinically infected wound, not for every ulcer. Debridement, drainage, pressure relief, perfusion, glycemic management, and follow-up are coequal parts of care.

Part 7 — Osteomyelitis: Think Beyond the Surface

Consider osteomyelitis when an ulcer is deep, chronic, recurrent over a bony prominence, exposes or closely approaches bone, fails to improve as expected, or is accompanied by concerning infection features. Initial studies and imaging should answer a clinical question and be coordinated with the multidisciplinary plan. A superficial swab is not a substitute for thoughtful evaluation of deep infection. Avoid both errors: dismissing a high-risk deep ulcer as superficial and labeling every chronic ulcer osteomyelitis without evidence.

Part 8 — Offloading Is Treatment, Not an Optional Extra

If repetitive pressure is driving a plantar neuropathic ulcer, wound dressings and antibiotics alone cannot solve the mechanical problem. Offloading redistributes pressure so tissue can heal. The specific modality depends on ulcer location, ischemia, infection severity, fall risk, adherence, resources, and specialist guidance. The FNP should reinforce why the device or footwear plan matters and ask whether the patient can safely use it at home and work.

Callus, deformity, footwear mismatch, and inability to inspect the foot are modifiable risks. Coordinate podiatry, wound care, orthotics, diabetes education, and family support as appropriate. A plan that is medically ideal but impossible to use is not a complete plan.

Part 9 — Charcot Neuro-Osteoarthropathy: The Hot, Swollen Foot

Active Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy can present as a warm, swollen, red foot in a patient with neuropathy, sometimes with surprisingly little pain. It may be confused with cellulitis, gout, sprain, or DVT. New unilateral warmth, edema, erythema, temperature asymmetry, shape change, or instability in a neuropathic foot should trigger urgent consideration of Charcot and prompt immobilization/offloading and specialist-capable evaluation according to local pathways. Delayed recognition can lead to collapse, deformity, ulceration, and amputation risk.

Part 10 — Emergency and Urgent Red Flags

Emergency evaluation is needed for systemic toxicity, rapidly spreading infection, severe pain or pain out of proportion, necrosis, crepitus, bullae, hypotension, altered mental status, or suspected necrotizing infection. Urgent multidisciplinary evaluation is appropriate for a deep or infected ulcer, gangrene, new ischemic findings, rapidly worsening wound, suspected osteomyelitis, exposed deep structures, active Charcot concern, or inability to safely perform outpatient care. Do not wait for a scheduled annual exam when the foot is declaring an emergency.

Part 11 — Prevention Is a Repeatable Clinical Process

Teach daily inspection, clean and dry skin care, avoidance of barefoot walking, appropriate socks and shoes, early reporting of blisters or cuts, and podiatric support for nails, calluses, and footwear when indicated. Ask the patient to teach back the plan. Address smoking cessation, glycemic management, blood pressure, lipids, nutrition, vision, mobility, housing, cost, and transportation because these factors determine whether prevention is achievable.

A prior ulcer or amputation is a major warning sign for future risk. Patients with neuropathy, PAD, deformity, renal disease, or previous ulcer need more frequent surveillance and a clear team relationship—not less attention because the current skin is closed.

Part 12 — FNP Case: The Painless Plantar Ulcer

A 63-year-old with diabetes reports no pain but has a callused plantar ulcer discovered when a sock became wet. Examination shows reduced protective sensation and poor shoe fit. The FNP documents wound and perfusion findings, assesses infection clinically, addresses immediate offloading and podiatry/wound-care coordination, reviews daily inspection, and sets an early follow-up. The absence of pain is explained by neuropathy, not interpreted as low risk.

Part 13 — FNP Case: Infection Plus Ischemia

A patient with diabetes and known PAD has a toe ulcer with new drainage, dark tissue at the margin, diminished pulses, and worsening function. Treating infection without evaluating perfusion risks delayed limb-saving care. The FNP recognizes the combined threat, arranges urgent vascular and surgical-capable assessment, and ensures the handoff communicates infection severity, ischemic findings, diabetes history, and medication considerations.

FNP High-Yield Framework

  1. Inspect: entire foot, nails, interdigital spaces, callus, wound, drainage, deformity, temperature, and footwear.
  2. Test the drivers: sensation/neuropathy, perfusion/PAD, pressure/biomechanics, infection, and patient ability to carry out care.
  3. Describe objectively: location, dimensions, depth, tissue, drainage, periwound findings, pain, pulses, and function.
  4. Treat the whole mechanism: wound care plus offloading, infection care when clinically present, ischemia assessment, glycemic and risk-factor support.
  5. Escalate early: deep infection, ischemia, gangrene, osteomyelitis concern, active Charcot, rapid deterioration, or systemic illness needs urgent multidisciplinary care.

Take-Home Summary

Diabetes-related foot disease is a limb-preservation problem. Neuropathy hides injury, pressure sustains it, PAD prevents healing, and infection accelerates harm. The FNP improves outcomes by examining feet consistently, treating an ulcer as a structured syndrome rather than a skin defect, insisting on offloading and perfusion assessment when indicated, and escalating quickly for infection, ischemia, Charcot, or deep tissue involvement.

Educational note: This lesson supports clinical reasoning and does not replace individualized diagnosis, wound-care protocols, current prescribing information, procedure training, vascular/podiatry/surgical guidance, or emergency evaluation when red flags are present.
